content: The use of diagnostic tools such as Xpert MTB/RIF and urine LAM (lipoarabinomannan assay) is critical because they provide significant advantages over other diagnostic methods. These tools enhance the accuracy and efficiency of tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, particularly in individuals co-infected with HIV. Understanding the burden of TB among people living with HIV is essential for guiding program management and planning. This knowledge helps in designing targeted interventions to address the dual epidemic of TB and HIV. In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) updated its guidelines for monitoring and evaluating collaborative TB/HIV activities. These guidelines recommend specific indicators for routine data collection, reporting, and utilization. These indicators are vital for identifying gaps in the TB detection cascade across all countries, with a particular focus on high-burden TB/HIV settings. For people living with HIV who are newly initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), routine TB screening is recommended. Ongoing TB screening is also advised for individuals on ART to ensure early detection and management of TB. Monitoring the entire cascade of care for HIV-associated TB is crucial. This includes screening, testing, prevention, and treatment. Countries are encouraged to define standard indicators across all relevant health information systems to track key TB and HIV interventions, as well as other co-morbidities. TB and HIV programs should conduct joint routine reviews of cascade data to ensure data quality and to use this information to improve program outcomes. This collaborative approach enhances the effectiveness of interventions and ensures that resources are allocated efficiently. Pregnant women living with HIV are at high risk of transmitting the virus to their infants during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. The prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) cascade encompasses a range of services, including primary prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and retention of HIV-positive mothers on ART to prevent transmission to their children. It also includes ensuring safe delivery, optimizing infant feeding practices, and tracking exposed infants throughout the exposure period to ensure early diagnosis and treatment of those who become infected. With the global shift toward simplified interventions based on lifelong maternal ART and rapid initiation of treatment, it is now feasible to virtually eliminate new HIV infections in infants while ensuring the health of mothers. However, some infants may enter PMTCT services late or remain outside these services while accessing other health services. Therefore, supporting infant HIV diagnosis wherever possible is critical. The PMTCT cascade spans multiple service delivery points and prolonged periods, requiring data collection from antenatal care visits, labor and delivery, HIV care, and postpartum and child health visits. Tools for data collection must align with patient care workflows and enable tracking of mother–baby pairs across service points. Strategic information systems for vertical transmission (VT) rely on robust systems for assigning unique identifiers to link records of mothers and their infants, integrating HIV information into existing maternal and child health (MCH) records, or using electronic systems to facilitate this process. As countries scale up PMTCT programs, they must invest in improving data completeness during the postnatal cascade. Monitoring retention and adherence to ART throughout the VT risk period becomes increasingly critical as new guidelines for maintaining mothers on ART are adopted. Historically, monitoring ART coverage and tracking final infant HIV outcomes have been weak areas in measuring the cascade. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in pregnant women are of significant public health importance due to their potential to cause stillbirth, prematurity, low birth weight, neonatal death, and diseases such as congenital malformations, ophthalmia, and pneumonia in newborns. However, recommendations for STI testing during pregnancy are generally limited to syphilis, as low-cost, simple, and high-performing diagnostics for gonorrhea and chlamydia are not yet widely available. Surveillance and monitoring of syphilis in pregnancy are particularly important in light of global and regional initiatives for the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of syphilis. Building on systems for collecting, reporting, and analyzing indicators for vertical transmission of HIV, countries can strengthen data to track their efforts to prevent congenital syphilis. Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in lowand middle-income countries. Of the over 300,000 women who die from cervical cancer each year, more than 85% are in these regions. Deaths are projected to rise by 50% by 2030 unless urgent and intensified action is taken. Women living with HIV are at significantly higher risk of developing cervical cancer due to persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infections and more rapid progression to cervical pre-cancer and cancer. Co-infection with other sexually transmitted agents, such as herpes simplex, chlamydia, and gonorrhea, further increases the risk of persistent HPV infection and cervical cancer development. New technologies, such as rapid single syphilis and dual HIV/syphilis tests, as well as the WHO initiative for the elimination of cervical cancer through HPV vaccination and screening, underscore the need for renewed focus on the prevention, detection, and appropriate treatment of STIs. Surveillance and monitoring are critical components of STI control programs. Prioritized STI program indicators reflect the importance of addressing severe morbidity and mortality related to STIs. Countries are advised to use indicators of syphilis screening coverage and treatment coverage in antenatal care (ANC) for basic monitoring and management of EMTCT of syphilis programs, as well as for validation purposes. In countries with concentrated and lower-burden epidemics, additional STI indicators may be relevant. For example, the seroprevalence of syphilis among sex workers and men who have sex with men are considered core indicators for guiding national responses to STIs. Data on these populations can be obtained through routine health information systems, sentinel surveillance, or special surveys. Clear case definitions are critical for ensuring the quality of case reporting, and all probable and confirmed cases should be reported. Routine STI prevalence assessments in the general population, conducted every three to five years, provide more reliable estimates of the burden of STIs than case reporting. Prevalence data serve multiple purposes, including developing national estimates of STI prevalence and incidence, identifying high-risk population groups, guiding funding and resource allocation, and monitoring the effectiveness of STI and HIV prevention programs.
